parts.title: Campus Conversation: Printing at the Computer Lab
script: Narrator
Listen to a conversation between a student and a computer lab assistant.
Man
Hi. I need to print my history paper. Is this the right place?
Woman
Yes. This is the main computer lab. You can print here if you have pages left on your student account.
Man
How many pages do I get?
Woman
Every student gets one hundred free pages each semester. After that, you pay five cents per page.
Man
I think I still have pages left. How do I check?
Woman
Log in at any lab computer and click Print Balance in the top corner. It shows how many pages you have left.
Man
Great. My paper is twelve pages, and I need two copies. Can I print on both sides of the paper?
Woman
Yes. Choose double-sided in the print window. That uses fewer pages from your account.
Man
Perfect. Where do I pick up the pages after I send them?
Woman
The printer is against the back wall, next to the windows. Look for your name on the small screen.
Man
One more thing. I also have a color map for my paper. Can I print that in color?
Woman
Color printing is only available at the library, not here. This lab prints in black and white only.
Man
Okay. I'll print the paper here and take the map to the library. Thanks for your help.
Woman
You're welcome. Good luck with your paper.

questions.q: What is the conversation mainly about?
o: Printing a paper at the computer lab
questions.exp: The student asks how to print his history paper in the computer lab.

questions.q: How many free pages does each student get each semester?
questions.exp: The woman says every student gets one hundred free pages each semester.

questions.q: How much does a student pay for each extra page?
questions.exp: She says after the free pages are used, students pay five cents per page.

questions.q: Listen again: "Choose double-sided in the print window." Why does the woman say this?
o: To help him use fewer pages from his account
To say the printer is broken
To tell him he cannot print today
To ask him to leave the lab
questions.exp: She explains that printing on both sides uses fewer pages from his account.

questions.q: Where should the student pick up his printed pages?
o: At the printer against the back wall, next to the windows
questions.exp: She says the printer is against the back wall, next to the windows.

questions.q: What will the student probably do with the color map?
o: Print it in this computer lab
Take it to the library to print in color
questions.exp: He says he will print the paper here and take the map to the library after learning this lab prints only in black and white.

parts.title: Academic Lecture: Why Does Ice Float?
script: Narrator
Listen to part of a lecture in a science class.
Professor
Good morning. Today I want to talk about a simple question: why does ice float on water? Most solid things sink if you drop them into water. A rock sinks. A coin sinks. But ice floats. Why?
Professor
The answer has to do with density. Density is how much mass is packed into a certain amount of space. If something is less dense than water, it floats. If it is more dense than water, it sinks.
Professor
When most liquids freeze, they shrink. The pieces move closer together, so the solid is more dense than the liquid. Water is different. When water freezes, it expands. It takes up more space.
Professor

Why does water expand? Inside ice, water molecules form a loose pattern, like a honeycomb. There is extra empty space between the molecules. Because of that empty space, ice is about nine percent less dense than liquid water. That is why it floats.
Professor

This fact is very important for animals. In winter, lakes freeze from the top down. A layer of ice sits on the surface and acts like a blanket. The water below the ice stays liquid. Fish and other animals can live there through the cold months.
Professor
If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up. The ice would fill the lake, and many animals would not survive the winter.
Professor
So remember: water expands when it freezes, ice is less dense than liquid water, and that is why ice floats. Next time we will talk about how salt changes the freezing point of water.

questions.q: What is the lecture mainly about?
questions.exp: The professor says today she wants to talk about why ice floats on water.

questions.q: What is density, according to the professor?
o: How hot or cold something is
How much mass is packed into a certain amount of space
questions.exp: She says density is how much mass is packed into a certain amount of space.

o: It expands and takes up more space
It becomes heavier than a rock
questions.exp: She says water is different: when water freezes, it expands and takes up more space.

questions.q: About how much less dense is ice than liquid water?
o: It is more dense, not less dense
questions.exp: She says ice is about nine percent less dense than liquid water.

questions.q: Listen again: "A layer of ice sits on the surface and acts like a blanket." Why does the professor say this?
o: To explain how ice helps keep the water below liquid in winter
To say people should put blankets on lakes
To describe how to make a bed
To warn students not to swim in summer
questions.exp: She is explaining that surface ice protects the liquid water below so animals can live there in winter.

questions.q: How does the professor organize the lecture?
o: She only lists types of rocks
She tells a story about a fishing trip
She defines density, explains why water expands when it freezes, then shows why this matters for lake animals
She compares ice only to metal
questions.exp: She first defines density, then explains that water expands into a loose pattern, then describes how floating ice protects animals in lakes.
